newsitem.title: RUSSIA: New Russian space team sure of restoring Mir power.
newsitem.headline: New Russian space team sure of restoring Mir power.

text.p: The commander of a relief crew for the Mir space station said on Sunday he was "absolutely sure" they would be able to restore power to the stricken craft.
Commander Anatoly Solovyov and flight engineer Pavel Vinogradov will blast off for Mir aboard a Soyuz spacecraft on Tuesday to relieve the crippled space station's tired and accident-prone crew.
On August 20, the cosmonauts are scheduled to don spacesuits and enter Mir's punctured and airless Spektr module to try to reattach interior cables to the solar panels outside.
The cables were severed when the current crew fled Spektr on June 25 after it was punctured by a Progress cargo craft during a manual docking manoeuvre.
Spektr's solar panels, which provide up to half of the 11-year-old space station's power, were damaged in the collision.
"I am absolutely sure this operation will be a success," Solovyov told Russian Television in a live interview from the Baikonur cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.
He said a spacewalk on September 3 would determine how to proceed with mending the hole in the Spektr.
Earlier on Sunday, the Soyuz yjsy will take Solovyov and Vinogradov to Mir was placed on a launch pad at Baikonur in preparation for Tuesday's launch.
A worker in grubby white overalls wiped down part of the Soyuz-U rocket booster before it was rolled out of a hangar along a railway track to the launch pad.
A hoist pushed the rocket, with a Soyuz TM-26 spacecraft on top, into vertical position under a glaring sun at the launch site, situated in the middle of parched steppe.
Mission Control had its first doubts about entrusting repair work to the current crew after commander Vasily Tsibliyev developed heart troubles.

Then a crew mistake of unplugging a vital computer, causing the station to lose its orientation for more than a day last month, convinced officials a fresh crew should undertake the repairs, which are vital for the future of the station.
The two Russian cosmonauts who came aboard on February 12 are scheduled to return to Earth on August 14. Solovyov and Vinogradov are expected to stay in orbit for about six months.
Physicist Michael Foale, from the U.S. space agency NASA, will stay on board until a U.S. shuttle arrives in September, when he will be replaced by American astronaut David Wolf.
